The quests are given by Riftwalker Maella or whatever her name is. It very much feels like someone prompted an AI for dialogue and accidentally had it mimic the wrong NPC. During the Omnium questchain, there’s also a part early on in the Lycenium where as you kill the echoes, Rommath and Umbric make statements. But after one particular echo kill, the statement Umbric gives in the chat is clearly being said by Rommath in the audio file, and vice versa.

Again, I’ve seen all sorts of errors in the history of the game, but it’s just weird that twice in this patch I’ve seen a type of error that I can’t remember seeing before, of misattribution to the wrong NPC in dialogue.

posts.name: Username
posts.cooked:
Tiffany:

However some say that works, others say it doesn’t.

It does. But this is not free version of GPT grade output.

AI is not limited to one-page modules anymore. Modern coding agents can work across multiple files, run tests, inspect errors, revise code, and make repo-level patches.

But I still would not treat an AI agent as a software architect that you hand an entire ambiguous system to and then trust the result.

The sweet spot is still bounded work: “add this feature,” “fix this bug,” “refactor this subsystem,” “write tests for this API,” or “implement this module against this interface.”

The human still needs to own the architecture, invariants, data model, security assumptions, failure modes, and review process. Agents are good at producing code and iterating quickly when the target is clear.

They are much weaker when the problem is underspecified, spans product judgment, or requires long-term maintainability decisions.

To Phae’s question:

Could Blizzard use AI to suggest a rough storyline that could plausibly map to all that is known of Warcraft Lore and also comply with the game’s requirements for engagement?

Certainly.

Did they use it? Not officially.

AI is a 3rd rail for too many of this games older customers. They wouldn’t risk this cash cow that way. They would test broad AI involvement on low-impact games - probably one with a younger demographic - and study the impact.

Might a few of Blizzards writing team have “messed with” AI privately, at home, to kick around some story ideas?

I’ll guarantee it.

Splints:

Challenge accepted.

The Covenant of the Unclaimed Dawn

The first mistake was believing Xal’atath wanted the Sunwell. The second was believing she wanted it destroyed.

By the time the champions returned from the Voidspire, the wound was made. L’ura’s essence had been torn from Alleria. The Sunwell had darkened into something older and hungrier than corruption. Alleria Windrunner and High Exarch Turalyon had fallen into the black radiance beneath Quel’Danas. Arator was cast back into the world alone.

For one hour, Silvermoon held its breath. Then the withdrawal began.

Wards stuttered. Blood Knight prayers rang hollow. Magisters lost the rhythm of ancient spells. Children woke weeping from dreams of a dark sun under the sea.

Yet, the Darkwell kept answering. It did not cut Quel’Thalas off; it fed the land, but every thread of power came back changed by attention. Every spell felt watched. Every prayer returned with an echo. Every ward became both a defense and a question.

Rommath sealed the city beneath the emergency Nine Veils. Nightborne arcanists brought stabilizing draughts. Liadrin ordered the Blood Knights to stop drawing directly from the font. Umbric and the ren’dorei were allowed into restricted sanctums where, days before, they would have been killed for approaching.

Silvermoon endured by admitting that the Sunwell could no longer be trusted. That was Xal’atath’s first victory: not corruption, but doubt.

Every power in Azeroth rushed to answer the Darkwell’s question. The Blood Knights came with wounded faith; the Magisters with discipline; the void elves with forbidden expertise; the Army of the Light with holy vengeance. The Amani came with oaths older than Silvermoon. The haranir came because the roots beneath the world were recoiling. And Arator came because his parents had vanished into it.

Beneath the city, the Sunstrider Omnium awakened.

Dath’remar had built it to classify magic. Rommath saw inheritance; Umbric saw danger; Xal’atath saw purpose. She had not broken the relic; she had let it work. It recorded every barrier of Light, every void rift sealed, every loa rite invoked, and every rootway stirred. It measured not force, but fear. It learned what mortals reached for when afraid.

The Omnium was no longer studying magic. It was studying allegiance: not what power mortals held, but what power they would surrender to under fear.

Naigtal had been the first rehearsal: life commodified, measured as stock. Val had been the second: ruin militarized, accepting command when survival was offered as order. Quel’Thalas was the third. Not life. Not ruin. Identity. Xal’atath had learned how worlds could be measured and commanded; now she would learn how a people could be made to choose the shape of its own cage.

The Darkwell reflected every fear. To Liadrin, a world where the Light failed. To Rommath, a kingdom undone because mastery faltered. To Umbric, an unwanted truth. To Turalyon’s soldiers, a delayed crusade. To Zul’jan, a chance to make old grievances holy. To Zul’jarra, the risk that peace would cost the Amani their memory. To Arator, it showed only silence.

Then Alleria spoke from inside the dark—not in words, but in a misfired void rift opening onto a hidden memory, and a shadowed arrowhead pointing away from a trap.

She was trapped in a recursion of possible truths. Every future showed betrayal; every hope became a door for the Void. So Alleria hunted. She hunted the point where prophecy became coercion, hiding a flaw in each reset—a pause, a wrong star, a memory of Arator as a child.

Turalyon stood in an endless dawn where every shadow was a threat and every doubt a weakness. To save her, he burned brighter, until protection became possession. Yet, he resisted with hesitation. Each time the Light commanded him to strike first, he waited one breath longer, asking the question the vision hated most: Safe for whom?

They were being edited. Xal’atath stripped them toward usefulness. Alleria became the argument that the Void tells the final truth; Turalyon became the argument that the Light must rule before darkness returns.

Their love survived without humility. It survived as a weapon.

At Zul’Aman, Zul’jan called for conquest. Let Silvermoon kneel.

Zul’jarra answered him with command: “If memory makes us only hunger, then we have learned nothing from what devoured us.”

The Amani would not forgive the elves to make the ritual easier. They demanded witness. At Jan’alai’s nesting ground, the new clutch cracked under flame and storm. The fire did not cleanse or conquer; it needed time. It was power that survived only by being carried forward.

The haranir understood. A font that feeds forever teaches hunger; a flame that must be tended teaches memory.

Beneath Harandar, the rootways opened. Champions descended through old scars: troll oaths, elven spellwork, Titan latticework, and roots of sleeping trees. At the threshold beneath Quel’Danas, Xal’atath waited. Not triumphant. Curious.

Around her, the Omnium unfolded in rings of impossible script, holding the world’s definitions.

Then the Darkwell opened, and Alleria and Turalyon emerged as a single contradiction: The Vow Made Weapon. It wore no stable shape—one moment a shield of burning dawn, the next a bowstring of living night. It spoke in their blended voices: I will burn the world before I lose you. I will make you mine.

The champions fought, but every attack made the Vow more certain. The golden pressure in the chamber thickened into command. Blood Knights heard orders in prayers; Magisters felt old hunger return; roots twisted away to protect the Worldcore.

Only when the champions stopped striking the Vow and instead severed the oaths feeding it did its shape begin to fail.

Then Arator stepped forward. He carried no shining blade, no void-touched bow, no cosmic relic. His armor was scarred, plain, and unlit. He did not choose between Light and Shadow. He broke Turalyon’s shield. He broke Alleria’s bowstring.

“I will not let your love be used as a law.”

The Vow screamed. Alleria fell from it gasping; Turalyon followed, his armor dimmed with terror. Arator stood before them not as a bridge, but as a boundary: “I am not what your Light and Shadow prove. I am what they failed to own.”

That was the first fracture. The second came as Rommath and Umbric turned on the Omnium. They changed the question. No longer would it classify magic by cosmic schools—Arcane, Light, Void. Those categories were for conquerors. The new taxonomy was older and harder: Freely chosen. Inherited. Coerced. Addictive. Imposed. Given in trust.

The Omnium convulsed. It could not understand power made conditional on consent. The Darkwell brightened toward limit.

Liadrin lowered her hammer, and the forced radiance guttered: “The Light is not less holy because I will not make it a chain.”

Umbric placed his hand against the blackened current, starving the whispers: “The Void is not truth because it shows me fear wearing a thousand faces.”

Rommath’s voice cut through the chamber, and the arcane pressure dropped so sharply that half the Magisters staggered.

Thalyssra shattered her leyglass: “Survival is the gentlest name addiction ever wore.”

Shandris named the oldest elven wound—the hunger for perfect sources—and the Well’s horizon became visible.

Zul’jarra came forward. Zul’jan had already turned away. The ritual did not require agreement; it required truth. She placed Amani memory into the Omnium as binding witness: “This land remembers before you named it.”

Jan’alai’s flame was carried to the water, teaching that life was not a resource. The haranir drew the excess downward through the rootways—not into a Titan machine or cosmic gate, but back into place. Local. Finite. Held.

The Well tried to become a beacon. Light, Void, and old arcane hunger tried to answer. Arator answered instead: “No.”

No to corruption, to purification as conquest, to salvation requiring ownership, and to every power that mistook Azeroth for something waiting to be claimed.

Xal’atath struck at the Well and found it smaller.

The Sunwell did not blaze back to glory. It dimmed. Its dark radiance thinned; its golden light softened. Its waters still shone, but no longer infinitely, no longer as a gate or a promise that hunger could be sanctified. It could heal and defend, but it could not rule.

Xal’atath recoiled because the prize had been made less useful. Her smile faltered. The Blade of the Black Empire cracked from contradiction.

Through the fracture came a sound like old laughter, impossibly deep and near, rising from below.

Azeroth had heard a wound refuse to become a doorway.

Then Xal’atath was gone.

The sky over Quel’Danas changed to a bruised dawn. Silvermoon’s towers caught the pale light and did not gleam, but they endured.

At the edge of the diminished waters, Liadrin heard no command from the Light. Umbric heard no whisper from the Void. Rommath saw no infinite reservoir. Zul’jarra watched from a distance and offered no forgiveness, only the smallest nod that the elves had answered a wound without making it larger.

Alleria and Turalyon survived, but neither returned whole. Turalyon knew how easily protection became possession; Alleria knew that seeing every future became another blindness. Arator stood between them as a witness.

Rommath spoke bitterly: “We have lost a sun.”
Lor’themar answered: “No. We have survived one.”
Arator looked to the quiet waters: “And they survived what it became.”

The Sunwell was renamed Anar’alah Belore’s Rest. The Light at rest. Not dead. Not triumphant. At rest.

The Amani did not celebrate. The void elves were not welcomed with open arms. The Army of the Light left uneasy. The Blood Knights prayed before a silence they did not yet understand.

But for the first time since the Well of Eternity, an elven civilization had chosen not to define itself by an inexhaustible source.

Far below, Titan machinery stirred.

The Void had failed to claim the Well. The Light had failed to turn defense into mandate. The Omnium’s categories were broken, Amani memory was binding, and mortals had done something no ordering engine predicted.

They had made power conditional on consent.

To Azeroth’s defenders, this was victory. To the Titans, it was a system failure.

For the world had not fallen to the Void. It had begun to say no.

To develop it all the way into campaign quests, cinematics, encounter hooks, VO direction, and implementation documentation, then it stops being “a story pitch” and becomes production narrative work. That could easily become six figures or more.

I could work with AI to do the complete “assignment” - but bring your checkbook.

AI-assisted draft: 218 seconds of model time plus my steering and critique.

Blizzard-accountable equivalent: probably $100k–$350k to reach serious internal pitch quality, and $500k–$1.5M+ if carried through production documentation and implementation support by human writers.

The essential difference is liability. My AI draft cost almost nothing because nobody’s career, IP strategy, player trust, quest production schedule, cinematic budget, localization pipeline, or franchise continuity was on the line. A Blizzard version would be expensive because every sentence becomes a decision the studio has to own.

Then on top of that narrative, if you want to “put it into textboxes linked with appropriately placed NPCs and quest segments”?

Well, lets look at what it probably costs now (rough estimate):

Lean implementation using existing assets and tools: $250,000–$750,000

Blizzard-quality campaign finale implementation: $1 million–$3 million

If it includes bespoke cinematics, VO, new encounter support, new set pieces, major phasing, and full localization/LQA: $5 million–$15 million+

My best single-number estimate for the thing you described — “put it into textboxes linked with appropriately placed NPCs and quest segments” — is around:

$1.5 million to $2.5 million

That assumes it is not merely pasted into quest windows, but actually implemented as a polished WoW campaign chapter. That work would include narrative design, quest design, quest scripting, NPC placement, phasing, event triggers, objective design, gossip text, quest accept/turn-in text, ambient barks, raid intro/outro hooks, internal lore review, stakeholder revision, localization formatting, QA passes, bug fixing, and final polish.
